structured_output.summary:
I searched the outside sources that bear on the open nodes. There is no public CIFAR-100 recipe close to the tip. The public numbers are the 59.3 s ResNet9 baseline and the 8.11 s airbench96-style PR, so CIFAR-10 speedruns and Muon papers are the only references. Main findings:

(1) Noise and the margin (H4). Jordan's variance paper gives a per-run test-set sd of about sqrt(err/2n). That matches CIFAR-10 (about 0.15 pp at 6% error), and for CIFAR-100 at 25% error it implies about 0.35 pp per run. That works out to about 0.2 pp on an unpaired 3-seed mean and about 0.06 pp on the 40-seed judge. Short runs also have large distribution-wise variance. So E069's +0.24 pp, seen on seeds 0-2 and gone on 13 seeds, is the expected size of a re-draw.

(2) Whitening strength (H1.2.7, H1.9). On CIFAR-10 airbench (the MUD paper), Muon5 and Muon3 are equal (94.03 vs 94.02 ± 0.1). Weaker decorrelation (MUD) costs 0.6-0.7 pp. This independently supports the E065 lesson that weaker whitening hurts, and it makes stronger whitening an unlikely source of lasting gains.

(3) Cheaper Newton-Schulz (H2.4.5, H2.4.8). Turbo-Muon/AOL saved only 0.8% wall time on the H100 CIFAR-10 speedrun. Gram NS has a large FLOP cut on paper at aspect ratio 9 with T=3 (-57% naive, -29% with the restart needed for stability). But it needs fp16 and restarts, and it squares the condition number, which degrades exactly the small singular directions that whitening is meant to lift.

(4) Hiverge's exact settings. The weight-norm projection runs every 2+int(15·progress) steps, which is the H2.4.3 schedule. The whitening bias is trained for only 0.2 epoch, against 1 epoch on the tip. Muon also uses weight decay, and the 0.50→0.08 Frobenius schedule shrinks the update size (it is not RMS-matched). So E065 tested a different mechanism from Hiverge's.

(5) Muon-C. On a 3x3 grid it is an exact frequency-wise split, essentially the method E030 tested. It gains +0.6 pp on ImageNet-100 at 100 epochs but costs 1.36x per step. This fits a horizon-dependent reading of E030's -1.2 pp.

(6) Smaller items.
- Drop-Muon supports updating shallow layers less often as training goes on, but its CIFAR gains are small, and E064 shows mid-run thinning hurts here.
- airbench96_faster's data filtering (a 32/64/64 depth-2 proxy, keeping the hardest 50% of each batch) gave -21% only at 45 epochs.
- PyTorch Dynamo guards Python floats on their exact value, so an edited constant should trigger a recompile, not a silent no-op. If H1.6.6 holds, it is more likely a code-path bug than a compile artifact.
- The A100 PCIe judge has a 300 W cap against 400 W for SXM, so kernel choices tuned on the SXM may not transfer (H2.5.1).
- Fable's CIFAR-10 SOTA used 24→28→32 progressive resizing. Its precomputed augmentation, machine lottery and cooldown were flagged as specification gaming and should not be copied.

findings.source: arxiv 2304.01910 (Jordan, 'On the Variance of Neural Network Training with respect to Test Sets and Distributions', ICLR 2024), https://arxiv.org/html/2304.01910v3
findings.claim: Under class-wise calibration, expected test-set variance is about err/(2n) plus the distribution-wise variance. CIFAR-10 test-set std: 1.87% at 0 epochs, 0.56% at 4, 0.19% at 16, 0.15% at 64. Distribution-wise std is 0.52% at 4 epochs and 0.033% at 64. Short runs therefore carry real quality variance on top of test-set sampling noise. Applying the same formula to CIFAR-100 at ~25% error and n=10000 gives a per-run sd of about sqrt(0.25/20000) ≈ 0.35 pp, which is my extrapolation (the paper has no CIFAR-100 runs). That is about 0.2 pp on an unpaired 3-seed mean and about 0.06 pp on the 40-seed judge mean.
findings.relevance: Grounds the noise model in H4/H4.1. A recipe change re-draws every seed, so unpaired 3-seed deltas below ~0.3-0.4 pp are inconclusive. E069's +0.24 pp on seeds 0-2 against a 13-seed mean of ~0.7534 is a typical selection draw. Gating on a 13-seed estimate of ≥0.753 leaves roughly 3 sd of headroom for the 40-seed ≥0.75 judgment.

findings.source: arxiv 2603.17970 (MUD: MomentUm Decorrelation), CIFAR-10 AIRBench table, https://arxiv.org/html/2603.17970
findings.claim: On airbench (8 epochs): Muon3 0.9402±0.0011 in 2.969 s, Muon5 0.9403±0.0010 in 3.039 s, MUD1 0.9334±0.0014, MUD3 0.9339±0.0013. The authors write: 'increasing the strength of the orthogonalization/decorrelation step is not advantageous in this benchmark'. The weaker decorrelation (MUD) costs ~0.65 pp.
findings.relevance: This is outside evidence for the E065 lesson that whitening below Muon's default costs a lot. It also says that stronger-than-NS3 whitening gives ~0 on CIFAR-10. That fits E069's +0.24 pp vanishing on 13 seeds and lowers the prior that H1.2.7 (stronger whitening) is a real gain.

findings.claim: Gram NS iterates on X·Xᵀ. FLOPs for standard symmetric NS are T(3α+1)n³, for naive Gram (4T+3α−3)n³, and for stabilized Gram with one restart (4T+6α−6)n³. At α=9 and T=3 that is 84n³ vs 36n³ (−57%) vs 60n³ (−29%). It requires fp16 rather than bf16, because bf16 gives spurious negative Gram eigenvalues that blow up. It needs a restart after iteration 2 with Polar Express coefficients and a 1.05 safety factor, and the authors call it 'fundamentally more unstable'. Forming X·Xᵀ squares the condition number, and the authors say it is not suitable when an accurate polar factor is needed. Measured gains: 25% NS speedup for dense LLMs, up to 2x for MoE.
findings.relevance: For H2.4.8 the stable version saves ~29%, not ~45%. The tip's matrices are small (n=128-576), where launch and latency dominate. The squared condition number targets the small singular directions that the E065/E069 results show matter. The gate should check the singular-value fraction above 0.5, not just the max deviation.

findings.claim: AOL preconditioning lets 4 NS iterations match 5. On the CIFAR-10 94% speedrun (H100) it reached 94.03% vs 94.04%, with runtime 1.348 s vs 1.359 s: −0.8%.
findings.relevance: In a heavily optimized CNN speedrun, the published end-to-end saving is 0.8%, below H2.4.5's ≥1.2% bar. This lowers its prior further and argues for retiring it.

findings.claim:
Hiverge settings:
- Muon: lr 0.205, momentum 0.655, Nesterov, weight_decay 1.0418e-6×batch_size; the norm/projection runs with norm_freq = 2+int(15·progress).
- NS: coefficients (3.4576, −4.7391, 2.0843), 3 unrolled iterations, Frobenius target magnitude 0.5012→0.0786.
- SGD: lr 0.0573, momentum 0.825; head lr 0.5415.
- Run: bs 1536, 7.65 epochs, label smoothing 0.09.
- Whitening: bias trained for ceil(0.2·steps_per_epoch) steps; SVD-based init with eps 5e-4.
findings.relevance: Confirms the H2.4.3 projection schedule exactly. The whitening bias is trained for only 0.2 epoch, against 1 epoch on the tip (H2.4.2/E034), so moving the freeze earlier is a small untested systems cut. Hiverge's Frobenius schedule is not RMS-matched: it shrinks updates and pairs with a different lr, intermittent projection and weight decay. So E065 refuted an RMS-matched variant, not Hiverge's actual mechanism.

findings.claim: For a 3x3 kernel the 'critical Fourier grid' is exactly 3x3. Muon-C polarizes the 9 frequency-wise C_out×C_in DFT blocks independently and maps them back with an orthonormal inverse DFT, with RMS scaling matched to Muon. On ImageNet-100 at 100 epochs it scores ResNet-34 80.22 vs 79.64 for unfolded Muon, ResNet-50 79.88 vs 79.28, ConvNeXtV2-T 84.88 vs 84.62. Step time is 99.4 ms vs 86.0 ms (1.16x unfolded Muon). There is no CIFAR classification or speedrun result.
findings.relevance: E030 implemented essentially this method and lost 1.2 pp at 6.5 epochs. The published gains come from 100-epoch, 224 px runs, which supports a horizon- and resolution-dependent reading of E030. That direction stays closed for this regime, and the method also costs ~16% more optimizer time.

findings.source: lesswrong.com/posts/ymdHH2QcPJrw4CuDz (fable is sota at cifar speedrun and specification gaming)
findings.claim: Fable's CIFAR-10 SOTA (1.828 s vs Hiverge's 1.98 s, −7.6%) came mainly from progressive resizing: 24 px, then 28 px after a few epochs, then 32 px. Pooling, CUDA-graph and optimizer-fusion work added the rest. The post flags three specification-gaming moves: all 9 epochs of augmented data precomputed untimed in setup, filtering for faster Modal hosts (1.726 s), and a 60 s untimed GPU cooldown (~9 ms).
findings.relevance: Independent support for the H2.3/H6 curriculum, which the tip already has in a cheaper form (20/28/32). Precomputing augmentation in build() and cooldowns would break RULES.md here (no real data in build; no sleeps), so the 'systems' gains in Fable's number should not be copied.

findings.claim: Randomized progressive training: each step updates a random suffix of layers [s..b], with no gradient below s. An 'epoch-shift' distribution moves probability mass from shallow to deep layers over training. In theory, full-network updates are optimal only if the first layer has the largest smoothness constant. Gains: up to 1.4x on MNIST and ~1.2x on Fashion-MNIST. On CIFAR-10 (3-layer CNN, bs 8192) the speedup is smaller.
findings.relevance: Supports H7's premise that shallow layers can get fewer updates late in training. But E064 showed mid-run random thinning of block 1 hurt (−0.54 pp), and the CIFAR gains here are small. This favours hard late freezes (E058) over stochastic suffix updates.

findings.claim: Data filtering: a 32/64/64 depth-2 proxy trains alongside the main model (gradient update every other step) and supplies per-batch losses. The main model backpropagates only the hardest 512 of each 1024 batch (50%). The main run is 45 epochs, and the result was 96% in 27.3 s vs 34.7 s for airbench96 (−21%). Records are timed on a 400 W A100 (SXM).
findings.relevance: The only published hard-example win is at a 45-epoch, 96%-accuracy horizon. At 6.75 epochs, where the tree finds steps are scarce early in training (E053), the prior for H1.4/H1.4.1 stays very low.

findings.source: PyTorch torch.compile recompilation docs / troubleshooting (docs.pytorch.org compile programming_model.recompilation; torch.compiler_troubleshooting)
findings.claim: By default Dynamo treats int/float Python values as constants and guards on their exact value. A changed float triggers a recompile (or an eager fallback past cache_size_limit), not silent reuse of the old graph. Wrapping values in tensors avoids the recompiles.
findings.relevance: Bears on H1.6.6. A changed lookahead decay or lr constant cannot be silently ignored by a compiled graph. If E028 really was a no-op, the cause is a code-path bug (an edited variable that is never read, or a value baked in elsewhere), not compile caching. Check the source and log the applied alpha rather than suspecting Inductor.

findings.source: datacrunch.io/blog/nvidia-a100-pcie-vs-sxm4-comparison; hyperstack A100 PCIe vs SXM comparison
findings.claim: A100 80GB PCIe is capped at 300 W against 400 W for SXM4, with 1,935 vs 2,039 GB/s memory bandwidth. Peak specs match, but SXM's extra power headroom sustains higher clocks under heavy load.
findings.relevance: For H2.5.1, max-autotune kernel choices and timings measured on the SXM dev box may not carry over to the power-capped PCIe judge. Absolute judge times may also run higher. This favours dropping SXM-specific autotuning unless its gain is clearly beyond jitter.

findings.claim: The only public CIFAR-100 speedrun numbers are the organizer baseline (ResNet9-style, width 64, 40 epochs, 75.36% in 59.30 s on A100 PCIe, two trials at 75.56/75.16) and an airbench96-style PR at 75.29% in 8.11 s on A100-SXM4. There is no public leaderboard.
findings.relevance: There is no external CIFAR-100 recipe near the tip (4.68 s), so further ideas must come from CIFAR-10 speedruns and optimizer papers. The baseline's two trials differ by 0.40 pp, consistent with the ~0.35 pp per-run sd estimate above.

findings.source: arxiv 2605.13079 (Spectral Flattening Is All Muon Needs); arxiv 2606.03899 (Denoise First, Orthogonalize Later) — abstracts only
findings.claim: (a) Muon's maximal stable step scales with the gradient's average singular value, not its largest, so the degree of spectral flattening sets the usable lr. (b) Momentum before orthogonalization acts as a spectral filter that widens the gap between signal and noise singular directions and gives provably better alignment than orthogonalizing first.
findings.relevance: (a) is consistent with the Muon lr having cliffs on both sides under the stronger Polar Express whitening (E075 at 0.12, E019 at 0.36): changing the flattening shifts the effective lr. (b) gives a mechanism for momentum mattering before NS; on this base momentum 0.6-0.8 was flat. Both are weak, abstract-level evidence with no CNN numbers.
